title: Exposure Reporting and Environmental Safety

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Report bloodborne and body fluid exposures promptly through the proper channels, including immediate first aid and escalation.
- Document exposure incidents accurately and objectively using the appropriate forms and logs while maintaining confidentiality.
- Maintain environmental safety by cleaning and disinfecting surfaces, managing spills, and segregating sharps and regulated waste correctly.
- Apply standard and universal precautions, including hand hygiene and personal protective equipment, to reduce exposure risk.
- Recognize the assistant's role in safety and escalation, leaving clinical and treatment decisions to licensed professionals.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Bloodborne pathogens are germs that live in blood and can make someone sick if that blood gets into a cut or a splash in the eyes. The three big ones we protect against are hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

### Question 2

The rule is like a safety checklist that bosses must follow so workers who touch blood or needles do not get sick.

### Question 3

An exposure control plan is like a game plan that explains where the risks are and what the team will do to stay safe.

### Question 4

Universal precautions means treating every drop of blood as if it could be germy, even if the person looks perfectly healthy.

### Question 5

Standard precautions are like wearing a seatbelt every time you ride in a car, not just when you think you might crash.

### Question 6

Some fluids, like sweat or tears, are usually safe unless blood is mixed in. But fluids like spinal fluid and certain reproductive fluids are treated as if they could carry germs.

### Question 7

If you poke yourself with a needle, wash the spot right away with soap and water, like cleaning any cut, and then go tell the person in charge.

### Question 8

If something splashes in your eye, you rinse it out with water right away, just like getting soap in your eye at bath time.

### Question 9

After a needle poke, you wash it with soap and water, but you do not squeeze it hard to make it bleed, because that can hurt the skin more.

### Question 10

After you wash the poke, you tell the boss right away, because the sooner you tell, the sooner you can get checked and helped.

### Question 11

After a needle poke, the worker can get checked by a doctor for free, and what they talk about stays private.

### Question 12

The office offers a free shot that protects workers from hepatitis B, and they get the chance to take it soon after starting the job.

### Question 13

If a worker says no thank you to the shot, they sign a paper, but they can change their mind later and still get it for free.

### Question 14

Whether to test the person whose blood was involved is a decision for doctors and the rules, not something the assistant does on their own.

### Question 15

The office keeps a list of needle accidents that notes what kind of needle it was and where it happened, so they can pick safer tools next time.

### Question 16

The needle-accident list is a private safety paper for the office, not part of the patient's medical folder.

### Question 17

The office keeps the paper that shows a worker finished safety training for three years.

### Question 18

An engineering control is a tool that makes the job safer, like a strong box for used needles so nobody gets poked.

### Question 19

A sharps box is like a strong, closed bucket for used needles that cannot poke through and that tells everyone it holds sharp, germy items.

### Question 20

Putting the cap back on a used needle with two hands is dangerous because you can poke yourself, so it is better to put it straight into the sharps box.

### Question 21

Used needles go straight into the strong sharps box right where they were used, not in the trash can.

### Question 22

When the needle box is full, you close it up and get a new one instead of squishing things down with your hand.

### Question 23

You never eat, drink, or put on lip balm where blood or needles are around, because germs could get into your mouth.

### Question 24

After you take off gloves, you still wash your hands, because germs can sneak onto your hands when the gloves come off.

### Question 25

Gloves are like a raincoat for your hands, but you still wash your hands after taking them off.

### Question 26

You put on a mask and goggles when something might squirt or splash, like a hose that could spray you.

### Question 27

When you take off dirty safety gear, you take off the dirtiest parts first and then wash your hands, so you do not spread germs onto yourself.

### Question 28

Before cleaning up blood, you put on gloves first, like putting on oven mitts before touching a hot pan.

### Question 29

To clean up blood, you use a special germ-killing cleaner, like using strong soap to clean a really messy spill at home.

### Question 30

You suit up, wipe up the mess, clean the spot with germ killer, and throw away the dirty towels in the right bag.

### Question 31

Broken glass is picked up with a brush and dustpan, like a janitor would, never with your fingers.

### Question 32

Regulated waste is the germy stuff like blood or things soaked in blood that needs special handling, unlike clean paper or empty boxes.

### Question 33

Things soaked in blood go into a special red bag with a germ warning sign, not the regular trash.

### Question 34

The biohazard sign is a warning sticker that means the box may hold germy items, so be careful.

### Question 35

Germy gloves go in the red bag, and the clean paper towel goes in the normal trash can.

### Question 36

A needle in a normal trash bag is like a thumbtack waiting to poke whoever picks up the bag, so it must go in the strong sharps box.

### Question 37

Dirty linens with blood are gently put into a special bag right where they were used, not shaken out or carried around loose.

### Question 38

Things everyone touches, like doorknobs, need regular cleaning with germ killer, like wiping the kitchen table after meals.

### Question 39

Cleaning is like wiping crumbs off the table, and disinfecting is like using a germ-killing spray afterward to make it extra safe.

### Question 40

The germ-killer spray needs to sit wet on the surface for a little while to do its job, like letting soap soak a greasy pan.

### Question 41

There are five times to wash your hands: before and after touching a patient, before a clean job, after touching anything yucky, and after touching things around the patient.

### Question 42

If your hands look dirty or have blood on them, you need real soap and water, not just the squirty hand gel.

### Question 43

When someone coughs, we help them cover it with a tissue and wash their hands, like sneezing into your elbow at school.

### Question 44

Needles and syringes are like one-time-use straws; once they are used, they are thrown away in the sharps box.

### Question 45

An exposure is when blood or body fluid touches a cut, an eye, or a needle poke, and that needs to be reported.

### Question 46

If blood lands on healthy, unbroken skin with no cuts, you wash it off with soap and water, and it is usually not a big deal like a cut or eye splash would be.

### Question 47

If you are not sure whether a splash or poke is a problem, tell the boss right away anyway, because it is better to check early than to wait.

### Question 48

After a risky needle poke, the sooner you tell, the sooner a doctor can decide if medicine would help, and fast is important.

### Question 49

You tell the person in charge at work, following the office's rules, not just a friend or someone at home.

### Question 50

If you are not sure whether you need medicine or a test, you let the boss and the doctor figure it out; you just report what happened.

### Question 51

Workers learn the safety rules when they start the job and then get a refresher every year, like a yearly fire drill.

### Question 52

The office keeps the worker's health papers for as long as they work there and thirty more years, because some sicknesses show up late.

### Question 53

The office keeps the needle-accident list for five years, like keeping important papers in a safe drawer for a long time.

### Question 54

A worker's health papers are private, like a secret diary, and are kept in a locked spot, not shown to everyone.

### Question 55

The boss gives workers the gloves and gowns for free, like a coach handing out team uniforms.

### Question 56

Workers do their part by following the safety rules, wearing the gear, and telling the boss if something happens.

### Question 57

Workers are allowed to look at the safety game plan anytime, like checking the rulebook before a game.

### Question 58

Keeping the work area tidy, like cleaning your room, helps stop people from tripping and keeps the needle box easy to reach.

### Question 59

The spill kit is like a cleanup backpack; you should know where it is and how to use the things inside before a mess happens.

### Question 60

Blood samples travel in a closed, labeled container that cannot leak, like a lunchbox with a tight lid.

### Question 61

Between each patient, the table gets wiped clean with germ killer, like cleaning a desk before the next person sits down.

### Question 62

Germs that live in blood are not caught by hugging someone or sharing a snack; they need to get into your blood through a poke, cut, or splash.

### Question 63

Hepatitis B is a tough germ that can live on surfaces for a while, but luckily there is a shot that protects workers from it.

### Question 64

If someone gets a bad needle poke, you help them wash it and tell the boss right away so a doctor can check them quickly.

### Question 65

If you have a cut on your finger, put on a bandage and gloves, like covering a scrape before playing outside.

### Question 66

Carry the needle box upright by its handle and never stick your hand inside, like carrying a full cup without spilling.

### Question 67

The special red bags are picked up by a licensed waste company, like the trash truck but for germy medical waste.

### Question 68

Never dig your hands into a trash bag, because a needle could be hiding inside like a thorn in a pile of leaves.

### Question 69

If blood gets on the counter, you clean it with germ killer right away, not next week.

### Question 70

Take gloves off by peeling from the wrist so the dirty outside never touches your clean skin, then wash your hands.

### Question 71

Write down just the facts about what happened, like a reporter: when, where, and how, without pointing fingers.

### Question 72

The accident report goes into the office's safety files, not into the patient's medical folder.

### Question 73

The safety plan gets checked and updated every year, and also whenever the office gets new tools or ways of working.

### Question 74

Safer needles are like scissors with rounded tips; they are designed so workers are less likely to get poked.

### Question 75

Scrub your hands with soap for about as long as it takes to sing the happy birthday song twice.

### Question 76

The hand gel works great when your hands look clean, but if they are dirty, you need soap and water.

### Question 77

You wear a gown or apron when things might splash, like wearing an apron while painting.

### Question 78

To protect your eyes from splashes, you wear goggles or a see-through face shield, like swim goggles.

### Question 79

Standard precautions are a whole safety toolkit: washing hands, wearing gear, using needles safely, and throwing germy trash away the right way.

### Question 80

If the needle box is broken, you stop using it and tell the boss so it gets fixed or replaced, like telling a teacher about a broken toy.

### Question 81

You wipe the crumbs and dirt off first, and then use the germ killer, because germs can hide under the dirt.

### Question 82

The needle box goes right where it is used, standing up and easy to reach, like a trash can next to your desk.

### Question 83

Instead of handing a used needle to someone, you put it down in a tray and let them pick it up, so nobody gets poked.

### Question 84

Clean, unsoiled gloves go in the regular trash, but germy ones go in the red bag; needles always go in the sharps box.

### Question 85

First wash the poke, then tell the boss, then write down the facts, and then go to the follow-up appointment.
